A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MM-Ego model, data engine and EgoMemoria benchmark. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable, including v1 Appendix A and v2 Appendices A–F. Retained and added material can be reliably distinguished.

before.justification: v1 reports original MM-Ego evaluations on EgoMemoria, EgoSchema and Video-MME, frame-count and sampling-parameter analyses, and qualitative predictions.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds an egocentric-only fine-tuning ablation and a comparison of generated QAs with and without video input.

M1.justification: The narration-based data engine, visual encoder and LLM, global glimpse/fallback procedure, pointer supervision and exploration–exploitation mechanism remain unchanged. Appendix D tests an alternative generator without adopting it; Appendix F describes possible future architectural extensions.

E1.justification: The training-data coverage and EgoMemoria, EgoSchema and Video-MME evaluations are retained. Appendix C selects from existing training data, while Appendix D examines the existing egocentric QA-generation task. Table 6 surveys other datasets without adding evaluations on them.

E2.justification: Appendix D newly compares the narration-only GPT-4o data engine against GPT-4o additionally receiving video frames, with outputs in Tables 8–9. The main comparator set in Tables 3–5 is unchanged; Table 7's LLaVA-OV data-mixture variant matches the earlier Ego SFT comparator.

E3.justification: Appendix C adds mixed-data versus egocentric-only fine-tuning controls for LLaVA-OV and MM-Ego. Appendix D adds a with/without-video generation comparison using 32 uniformly sampled 336×448 frames from one 30-second video. Previously stated main experimental settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 7 adds a focused training-data-mixture ablation, and Tables 8–9 add a single-clip case study testing whether visual input improves QA generation. The original frame-count, alpha-sensitivity, key-frame-selection and wearable-video analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests for the experimental results. The new ablation continues the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 7 adds egocentric-only MDA averages of 58.11 for LLaVA-OV and 63.78 for MM-Ego, alongside retained mixed-data averages of 55.97 and 61.27. These are results under additional training conditions. Tables 8–9 add generated QA examples; the original Tables 3–5 scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–3 and the mathematical descriptions of embeddings, selection and training are retained. No formal assumptions, proofs or derivations are added. The neuroscience analogy and proposed future extensions are conceptual discussions.

C1.justification: Dataset priority claims are narrowed: the abstract changes 'currently the largest' to 'one of the largest,' the introduction changes 'the first' to 'one of the first,' and the conclusion drops exclusive priority. The three central contributions remain the dataset, benchmark and Memory Pointer Prompting model.

C2.justification: Appendices C–F substantially expand interpretation: they discuss specialization versus general-video capability, labeling-model limitations, hallucination and computational costs, connections to visual-processing pathways, and strategies for longer videos. These broaden the explanatory scope without establishing implemented changes or validating every new interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses greedy decoding, an exact QA-generation prompt with example narrations, and the frame sampling and resolution used in the generation case study. Appendix B also reports 8,933 training videos. These add documentation without establishing changes to previously reported implementation settings.

R1.justification: Appendix B and Table 6 substantially expand research positioning. They explicitly acknowledge similarities to LLaMA-VID and the already-cited GroundVQA, distinguish dataset scale and duration coverage, and discuss concurrent HourVideo alongside broader video benchmarks. Appendix E adds neuroscience references and connections.

P1.justification: The title adds 'for Video QA,' selected abstract and contribution passages are edited, and Section 5 becomes a standalone conclusion. The original limitations paragraph moves to Appendix B; thematic appendices and an acknowledgment are added. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 5 replaces noun/verb pie charts with word clouds, Figure 1 receives revised labeling and caption wording, and Tables 6–9 are added. Existing model diagrams, qualitative examples and main result-table structures are largely retained, with localized resizing and page reflow.

improvement.justification: v2 improves attribution and calibrates novelty claims, adds a useful training-mixture control, and discloses an explicit generation prompt while retaining the original method and results. The gains are limited: the generation comparison is a single unscored example, Table 7 does not measure the asserted general-video degradation, and Appendix B contradicts Table 6 on HourVideo's QA count (121,976 versus 12,976). These weaknesses temper the overall improvement.
